catalog.label: Base
catalog.description: Baseline security controls for PAN-OS firewalls.

controls.name: LDAP Server Profiles Require SSL/TLS
controls.description:
An LDAP bind carries the bind account's credentials. Without SSL/TLS they cross the network in the clear, and anyone on the path reads the account that can enumerate the directory.

ABSENT MEANS ON. `ssl` is IMPLICIT YES - measured 2026-09-09 by writing a profile without the key and opening it in the UI, where the box renders checked. So this fires only on an EXPLICIT `no`. Reading the key as "absent means off" would report every profile that has never been edited as cleartext.

EVERY QUERY CLAUSES ON `kind`. Six kinds share one table and the measured implicit values live on every row, so a query on this column alone would fire on kinds it means nothing for.

Applies to profiles used for administrator authentication, User-ID group mapping and GlobalProtect alike - the profile does not know what will reference it.
controls.rationale: A cleartext bind hands over the account that can read the whole directory.
controls.audit: Device > Server Profiles > LDAP > <profile> > Require SSL/TLS secured connection.
controls.remediation: Tick Require SSL/TLS secured connection, and pair it with port 636 and certificate verification (PAN-AAA-002) - encryption without verification still accepts any certificate presented.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: LDAP profiles with SSL/TLS explicitly off.

controls.name: LDAP Verify Server Certificate
controls.description:
Encryption without verification stops an eavesdropper and not an interceptor: the firewall will complete a TLS handshake with whatever presents itself, so a machine-in-the-middle collects the bind credentials and relays the session.

ABSENT MEANS OFF here, unlike its neighbour four lines up the same dialog. The Help says so outright - "Select this option (cleared by default)" - and the committed object omits it. So this fires on absence, and PAN-AAA-001 does not. Neighbouring checkboxes on one screen do not share a default.

EVERY QUERY CLAUSES ON `kind`. Six kinds share one table and the measured implicit values live on every row, so a query on this column alone would fire on kinds it means nothing for.

It fires whether or not SSL is on. A profile with neither has two things to fix and the remediation for this one is the same either way.
controls.rationale: TLS to an unverified server authenticates nothing.
controls.audit: Device > Server Profiles > LDAP > <profile> > Verify Server Certificate for SSL sessions.
controls.remediation: Import the CA that issued the directory server's certificate into the firewall certificate store, then tick Verify Server Certificate.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: LDAP profiles not verifying the server certificate.

controls.name: RADIUS Uses Strong Authentication Protocol
controls.description:
PAP sends the password obscured only by the shared secret, so anyone who learns the secret - or captures enough traffic - recovers credentials. CHAP removes that, and PEAP-MSCHAPv2 or EAP-TTLS put the whole exchange inside TLS with server-certificate validation.

TWO TIERS, and they are the corpus's own: CHAP is the MINIMUM and PEAP-MSCHAPv2 the PREFERRED. PAP reports at the control's `high`; CHAP reports `medium` through the second query below. Anything TLS-wrapped passes.

NO IMPLICIT VALUE IS NEEDED. `protocol` is refused at COMMIT if omitted, so a RADIUS profile that exists always states one - measured, not assumed.

EVERY QUERY CLAUSES ON `kind`. Six kinds share one table and the measured implicit values live on every row, so a query on this column alone would fire on kinds it means nothing for.
controls.rationale: The protocol decides whether a captured RADIUS exchange yields a password.
controls.audit: Device > Server Profiles > RADIUS > <profile> > Authentication Protocol.
controls.remediation: Move to PEAP-MSCHAPv2 or EAP-TTLS, which needs a certificate profile on the RADIUS profile so the server certificate is validated. CHAP is the floor, not the target.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: RADIUS profiles below the preferred protocol.

queries.name: Meets the minimum, misses the target
queries.short_description: CHAP - the corpus minimum, not its preferred.

controls.name: TACACS+ Profile Hardening
controls.description:
TACACS+ encrypts the body of its packets with the shared secret, but PAP still carries the password in a form recoverable by anyone holding that secret. CHAP is the corpus minimum and its preferred value both.

THE CORPUS NOTE'S WIRE FORM IS WRONG FOR THIS KIND. It says to write `<protocol><CHAP/></protocol>`; measured 2026-09-09, tacplus stores `protocol` as TEXT and refuses the element form - "tacplus -> <name> -> protocol is invalid". The RADIUS profile beside it does take the element form, and `action=complete` returns the same value list for both, so the schema oracle cannot tell them apart.

The enumeration measured on this platform is CHAP | PAP. The corpus mentions `auto` on 12.1; it is not offered here.

EVERY QUERY CLAUSES ON `kind`. Six kinds share one table and the measured implicit values live on every row, so a query on this column alone would fire on kinds it means nothing for.
controls.rationale: PAP inside TACACS+ is recoverable by anyone holding the shared secret.
controls.audit: Device > Server Profiles > TACACS+ > <profile> > Authentication Protocol.
controls.remediation: Set the protocol to CHAP. Pair it with use-single-connection and a per-device shared secret, and reach the TACACS+ server over the management network only.

controls.name: SAML IdP Certificate Validation Enabled
controls.description:
With validation off the firewall accepts a SAML assertion signed by anything. That is CVE-2020-2021, an authentication bypass: forge an assertion and become any user the IdP could have named.

ABSENT MEANS ON. `validate-idp-certificate` is IMPLICIT YES - measured by writing a profile without the key and opening it in the UI, where the box renders checked. So this fires only on an EXPLICIT `no`, which is somebody having turned it off. Reading absence as "off" would report every unedited SAML profile in an estate as bypassable.

EVERY QUERY CLAUSES ON `kind`. Six kinds share one table and the measured implicit values live on every row, so a query on this column alone would fire on kinds it means nothing for.

A bare saml-idp profile cannot exist: `certificate`, `entity-id`, `sso-url` and `sso-bindings` are all refused at commit if missing, so there is always an IdP certificate for this setting to validate.
controls.rationale: Validation off is an authentication bypass with a CVE attached.
controls.audit: Device > Server Profiles > SAML Identity Provider > <profile> > Validate Identity Provider Certificate.
controls.remediation: Tick Validate Identity Provider Certificate. It needs the IdP's signing certificate to be CA-issued and a certificate profile holding that CA; a self-signed IdP certificate is the case the CVE mitigation assumes.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: SAML profiles with IdP certificate validation explicitly off.

controls.name: SAML Message Signing Enforced
controls.description:
Signing the firewall's own authentication requests protects the outbound leg: without it an attacker can tamper with a request in flight. The corpus sets no MINIMUM here - certificate validation already covers the inbound assertion - so this is a preferred-value control and carries its preferred-gap severity.

ABSENT MEANS ON, measured the same way as PAN-AAA-008. Fires only on an explicit `no`.

EVERY QUERY CLAUSES ON `kind`. Six kinds share one table and the measured implicit values live on every row, so a query on this column alone would fire on kinds it means nothing for.

The signing certificate itself is configured on the authentication profile, not here, so a finding on this leaf is about the flag rather than about a missing certificate.
controls.rationale: An unsigned request leg is tamperable in flight.
controls.audit: Device > Server Profiles > SAML Identity Provider > <profile> > Sign SAML Message to IdP.
controls.remediation: Tick Sign SAML Message to IdP, and set a Certificate for Signing Requests on the authentication profile that uses this IdP.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: SAML profiles not signing messages to the IdP.

controls.name: Authentication Profile Allow Lists Scoped
controls.description:
An authentication profile's allow-list decides WHICH users may authenticate through it. Set to `all`, every user the method can reach is admitted - so on a profile bound to administrators, one directory-wide phishing success reaches the management plane.

SCOPED TO ADMINISTRATIVE PROFILES, which is the corpus's own scoping and the same ruling Jason gave for PAN-AUTH-020: "GlobalProtect, Captive Portal, and even unused authentication profiles are very much separate controls." A profile counts as administrative when something under `mgt-config/users` or `deviceconfig/system` names it - derived from the referrer walk PAN-AUTH-025 already performs, which is what turns "which profiles do administrators use" from an open question into a column.

THE SUBJECT IS THE PROFILE, not the administrator. PAN-AUTH-019 and 020 moved to the account because their assertions were about a person's exposure; this one is about a property OF the profile and the remediation is on the profile, so it stays here. Jason, 2026-09-09: the per-user ruling "is not a general rule. The other authentication profile controls should stay profile-centric."

`all` is not a value somebody chose - it is what the Add form leaves behind, and all nine profiles on the lab carry it. That is why the administrative clause is load-bearing rather than decorative: without it this fires on every authentication profile in every estate.
controls.rationale: An admin-bound profile open to the whole directory turns one phished user into management-plane access.
controls.audit: Device > Authentication Profile > <profile> > Advanced > Allow List, for each profile an administrator authenticates through.
controls.remediation: Replace `all` with the named administrator group, sourced through LDAP group mapping over a verified TLS connection (PAN-AAA-001 and 002). Where the profile serves both administrators and users, split it - the allow-list is the only thing separating them.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Administrator-bound profiles whose allow list is `all`.

controls.name: Administrator MFA Delivered by RADIUS or SAML
controls.description:
An MFA server profile is the firewall's DIRECT integration with a vendor's API - Duo v2, Okta Adaptive, PingID or RSA SecurID - and the platform invokes it for END-USER authentication through Authentication Policy only. It is not invoked for administrator login to the web interface, and not for GlobalProtect.

So an authentication profile that an administrator authenticates through, carrying an MFA factor, does not give that administrator a second factor. It gives the configuration the APPEARANCE of one. That is the finding: not missing MFA, which is PAN-AUTH-019's subject, but MFA that is configured, visible in the UI, reported by every config audit as present, and silently ignored at the moment it would matter.

Three passages say so in different words. Guide p.221: "For remote user authentication to GlobalProtect portals and gateways and for administrator authentication to the Panorama and PAN-OS web interface, the firewall integrates with MFA vendors using RADIUS and SAML only." Help p.941 says the API integration enforces MFA "through Authentication policy for end-user authentication only (not for GlobalProtect authentication or administrator authentication)". Help p.839 says it of the Factors tab itself: "Although you can configure additional factors, they will not be enforced for these use cases." None of them was trusted alone: the same Help was measured wrong twice this month on the lockout fields. Measured 2026-09-10: an administrator bound to a profile whose one factor points at an unresolvable Duo host logged in instantly with the password alone.

ADMINISTRATIVE is the whole control. The identical profile serving Authentication Policy is correct configuration and must not fire - which is why the lab carries the pair, two profiles differing in nothing but whether an administrator is bound to one.
controls.rationale: Administrators appear to have a second factor and do not have one.
controls.audit: Device > Authentication Profile > <profile> > Factors, for each profile named under mgt-config/users or deviceconfig/system. Any MFA server profile listed there is inert for administrator login.
controls.remediation: Deliver the second factor through the first factor instead: point the profile's Type at a RADIUS server profile for the MFA vendor's RADIUS endpoint, or at a SAML IdP that enforces MFA. Then remove the Factors entry, which is doing nothing. Keep vendor-API MFA profiles for Authentication Policy, where they work.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Administrator-bound profiles with additional factors enabled and at least one listed.

controls.name: Authentication Sequence Fallback Order Safe
controls.description:
An authentication sequence tries its profiles top to bottom until one succeeds, so a member whose method is `local-database` or `none` is a way in with a credential the firewall itself holds - reached whenever everything above it fails, including when the external servers are down or unreachable. On a sequence an ADMINISTRATOR authenticates through, that is a management-plane login that bypasses the identity system, and an attacker who can knock the external servers over can force it.

SCOPED TO ADMINISTRATIVE SEQUENCES, the corpus's own wording: "No admin-facing authentication sequence falls back to local-database." A sequence counts as administrative when something under `mgt-config/users` or `deviceconfig/system` names it - every administrative binding accepts a sequence, measured 2026-09-11, including both device-wide leaves, which REFUSE a local-database profile but accept a sequence containing one. The identical sequence behind captive portal is other people's control, and the lab carries the pair.

THE VENDOR RECOMMENDS THIS SHAPE. Help p.843: "Make the local authentication profile the last profile in the sequence so it's only used if all external authentication methods fail." The corpus excepts documented break-glass; whether it is documented is not in the configuration, so the control reports and the consultant decides.

`exit-sequence-on-failure` (implicit NO, measured) does not clear it: it stops the sequence when credentials match a profile and fail, and a server that does not answer is not a failed match.
controls.rationale: A local fallback on an administrator sequence is a login the identity system cannot revoke.
controls.audit: Device > Authentication Sequence - for each sequence named under an administrator account or Device > Setup > Management > Authentication Settings, list the profiles in order and each one's Type.
controls.remediation: Remove local-database profiles from administrator-facing sequences. Keep break-glass as a separate, documented local account with its own profile rather than a silent fallback inside every administrator's login path.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Administrator-bound sequences with a local-database or none member.

controls.name: Unused AAA Server Profiles Removed (Hygiene)
controls.description:
A server profile nothing references is configuration debt: a live definition nobody audits, often pointing at an AAA server that was decommissioned, and one binding away from being used.

AN UNUSED CLAIM IS ONLY AS GOOD AS THE LIST OF HIDING PLACES, so the reference count comes from walking the WHOLE merged payload for `server-profile` rather than visiting known paths - the same walk PAN-AUTH-025 uses, and the same reason: a path an enumeration missed would report an in-use profile as unused, and the remediation here is deletion.

A reference from inside a vsys resolves to that vsys's profile of the name when one exists and to the shared one otherwise. Attributing it wrongly is two errors at once - the real profile reports unused and the same-named orphan reports in use.

This one does NOT clause on kind: an orphan is an orphan whatever it authenticates.
controls.rationale: An orphaned AAA profile is a live definition nobody is maintaining.
controls.audit: Device > Server Profiles - for each profile, search the configuration for its name.
controls.remediation: Delete the profile. PAN-OS refuses a delete that would break a reference and names the referring path, so a refusal is itself the answer to 'is this really unused'.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Server profiles nothing on the appliance references.

controls.name: Enable Minimum Password Complexity Enforcement
controls.description: The master switch for the password-complexity engine. While it is off, every individual requirement on the device is stored but not enforced - a device can show a 12-character minimum and accept a one-character password.\n\nMeasured 2026-09-03: absent means OFF, and enabling it through the UI writes ONLY the flag. The zeros shown on that form are rendered defaults, not stored values, so the easiest path through the GUI produces a policy that is switched on and requires nothing.
controls.rationale: Administrative passwords are the last barrier when every other control has been bypassed, and a firewall's administrator holds the policy that protects everything behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Minimum Password Complexity > Enabled.
controls.remediation: Tick Enabled, and set the individual requirements in the SAME change - enabling alone leaves every requirement at zero.

controls.name: Minimum Password Length
controls.description:
Enforces a floor on local administrator password length. The corpus minimum is 12 (CIS) and the preferred value 15 (DISA STIG).

The configurable range is 6 to 16, so a zero is reachable only by ABSENCE - a deliberate zero cannot be written. A stored 0 for this key therefore always means never configured.

These settings are INERT while password complexity is disabled - the device enforces none of them. That does not change this finding, which is true either way, but it does change the remediation: fixing this alone accomplishes nothing until PAN-AUTH-001 is also fixed.
controls.rationale: Administrative passwords are the last barrier when every other control has been bypassed, and a firewall's administrator holds the policy that protects everything behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Minimum Password Complexity > Minimum Length.
controls.remediation: Set Minimum Length to at least 12; 15 where clients allow it. The maximum the device accepts is 16.

controls.name: Require Uppercase Letters in Passwords
controls.description: At least one uppercase letter, widening the effective character set against guessing.\n\nThese settings are INERT while password complexity is disabled - the device enforces none of them. That does not change this finding, which is true either way, but it does change the remediation: fixing this alone accomplishes nothing until PAN-AUTH-001 is also fixed.
controls.rationale: Administrative passwords are the last barrier when every other control has been bypassed, and a firewall's administrator holds the policy that protects everything behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Minimum Password Complexity > Minimum Uppercase Letters.
controls.remediation: Set Minimum Uppercase Letters to at least 1.

That does not change this finding, which is true either way, but it does change the remediation: fixing this alone accomplishes nothing until PAN-AUTH-001 is also fixed.

controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Minimum Password Complexity > Minimum Special Characters.
