That does not change this finding, which is true either way, but it does change the remediation: fixing this alone accomplishes nothing until PAN-AUTH-001 is also fixed.
controls.rationale: Administrative passwords are the last barrier when every other control has been bypassed, and a firewall's administrator holds the policy that protects everything behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Minimum Password Complexity > Block Username Inclusion.
controls.remediation: Tick Block Username Inclusion (including reversed).

controls.name: New Password Minimum Character Difference
controls.description: Requires characters to change on rotation, stopping trivial increments like Password1 to Password2. Corpus minimum 3, preferred 8.\n\nThese settings are INERT while password complexity is disabled - the device enforces none of them. That does not change this finding, which is true either way, but it does change the remediation: fixing this alone accomplishes nothing until PAN-AUTH-001 is also fixed.
controls.rationale: Administrative passwords are the last barrier when every other control has been bypassed, and a firewall's administrator holds the policy that protects everything behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Minimum Password Complexity > New Password Differs By Characters.
controls.remediation: Set New Password Differs By Characters to at least 3; 8 approaches half of a 15-character password.

controls.name: Prevent Password Reuse (History Count)
controls.description: The number of previous passwords checked on change. Zero means the new password is checked against NO history, so the previous password can be set again immediately. Corpus minimum 5, preferred 24.\n\nThese settings are INERT while password complexity is disabled - the device enforces none of them. That does not change this finding, which is true either way, but it does change the remediation: fixing this alone accomplishes nothing until PAN-AUTH-001 is also fixed.
controls.rationale: Administrative passwords are the last barrier when every other control has been bypassed, and a firewall's administrator holds the policy that protects everything behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Minimum Password Complexity > Prevent Password Reuse Limit.
controls.remediation: Set Prevent Password Reuse Limit to at least 5; 24 defeats cycling through a small pool.

controls.name: Password Expiration Period
controls.description:
Bounds how long a leaked credential stays usable. The corpus minimum is 90 days and the preferred value 60.

This is the one setting on this form where BOTH ENDS are wrong. Zero means passwords NEVER expire, and a large value means they expire too rarely - so the control fires on 0 and on anything above 90, and passes between 1 and 90. A less-than comparison would have passed a 365-day expiry and failed the preferred 60.

These settings are INERT while password complexity is disabled - the device enforces none of them. That does not change this finding, which is true either way, but it does change the remediation: fixing this alone accomplishes nothing until PAN-AUTH-001 is also fixed.
controls.rationale: Administrative passwords are the last barrier when every other control has been bypassed, and a firewall's administrator holds the policy that protects everything behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Minimum Password Complexity > Required Password Change Period.
controls.remediation: Set Required Password Change Period to 90 days or fewer, and not to 0. Where MFA and breach monitoring are in place, review whether forced rotation is still the right policy for your standard - this control asserts the corpus floor.

controls.name: Password Expiration Warning Period
controls.description:
Days of warning before a password expires, so rotations happen deliberately rather than as lockouts. Corpus minimum 7, preferred 14.

Assessed independently of PAN-AUTH-010: a missing warning period is wrong whether or not passwords expire today, and it stays wrong the moment an expiry is set.

These settings are INERT while password complexity is disabled - the device enforces none of them. That does not change this finding, which is true either way, but it does change the remediation: fixing this alone accomplishes nothing until PAN-AUTH-001 is also fixed.
controls.rationale: Administrative passwords are the last barrier when every other control has been bypassed, and a firewall's administrator holds the policy that protects everything behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Minimum Password Complexity > Expiration Warning Period.
controls.remediation: Set Expiration Warning Period to at least 7 days; 14 gives distributed teams more runway. The maximum is 30.

controls.name: Disallow Post-Expiration Admin Logins
controls.description:
How many times an administrator may still log in after their password has expired. The secure value is ZERO, which is also the default - so this control fires only where somebody has deliberately allowed expired credentials to keep working.

The range is 0 to 3.

These settings are INERT while password complexity is disabled - the device enforces none of them. That does not change this finding, which is true either way, but it does change the remediation: fixing this alone accomplishes nothing until PAN-AUTH-001 is also fixed.
controls.rationale: Administrative passwords are the last barrier when every other control has been bypassed, and a firewall's administrator holds the policy that protects everything behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Minimum Password Complexity > Post Expiration Admin Login Count.
controls.remediation: Set Post Expiration Admin Login Count to 0. Before enforcing it, make sure a break-glass or console path exists - this setting can lock every administrator out of a device whose passwords have expired.

controls.name: Disallow Post-Expiration Grace Period
controls.description: Days during which an expired password still works. The secure value is ZERO, which is also the default, so this fires only where a grace window was deliberately configured.\n\nThese settings are INERT while password complexity is disabled - the device enforces none of them. That does not change this finding, which is true either way, but it does change the remediation: fixing this alone accomplishes nothing until PAN-AUTH-001 is also fixed.
controls.rationale: Administrative passwords are the last barrier when every other control has been bypassed, and a firewall's administrator holds the policy that protects everything behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Minimum Password Complexity > Post Expiration Grace Period.
controls.remediation: Set Post Expiration Grace Period to 0. As with the login count, confirm a break-glass path exists first.

controls.name: Failed Login Attempts Before Lockout
controls.description:
Locks an administrator account after N consecutive failed logins, which is what stops online password guessing and spraying.

BOUNDED AT BOTH ENDS, and the low end is not what it looks like. The device accepts 0 to 10. A 0 does not mean 'strict' - it means LOCKOUT IS DISABLED ENTIRELY, so it is the worst value available rather than the best, and it is also the implicit value: measured 2026-09-04 on the unconfigured Authentication Settings form. A comparison written as 'more than 5 is a finding' passes every unconfigured device in an estate.

The corpus grades 'more than 10' as high; the device grammar is 0-10, so that band cannot be reached. The reachable grading is 0 (sentinel, high), 1-5 (passes), 6-10 (medium).
controls.rationale: Administrative access to the firewall is access to every policy behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Authentication Settings > Failed Attempts.
controls.remediation: Set Failed Attempts to 5 or fewer; 3 is the common hardening target. Do not leave it at 0, which disables lockout. Pair it with a non-zero Lockout Time (PAN-AUTH-015) or a locked account releases immediately.

queries.name: Severity: 6 to 10
queries.short_description: failed attempts before lockout 6 to 10 — reported medium.

controls.name: Admin Account Lockout Duration
controls.description:
How long a locked administrator account stays locked. The device accepts 0 to 60 minutes.

ZERO IS THE STRONGEST VALUE HERE, which is the opposite of PAN-AUTH-014 on the same screen, and the reason the two cannot share a shape. The PAN-OS field help states it outright: "A value of 0 (default) means the lockout applies until another administrator manually unlocks the account" - and, explicitly, that failed-attempts set with lockout-time left at 0 locks the user until a manual unlock. So 0 is stricter than any duration, not weaker, and reporting it as "below 15 minutes" would flag the most restrictive setting available as a weakness.

The finding is therefore the EXCLUDED MIDDLE: 1 to 14 minutes - long enough to have been set deliberately, short enough not to throttle a guessing attack. 0 is also the implicit value, so an untouched device does not fire this. That is correct: with failed-attempts also 0 nothing ever locks, and PAN-AUTH-014 is the control that says so.

There is no severity scale, and none is needed - a 14-minute window has nothing to grade inside it.
controls.rationale: Administrative access to the firewall is access to every policy behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Authentication Settings > Lockout Time.
controls.remediation:
Set Lockout Time to at least 30 minutes; Palo Alto's own field help recommends 30 "to prevent continuous login attempts from a malicious actor", and the corpus floor is 15. The maximum is 60.

Leaving it at 0 is stronger still - the account holds until an administrator unlocks it - and is a legitimate choice. Understand the trade first: an attacker who can reach the login page can lock every administrator out and leave them there. Pair either choice with a non-zero Failed Attempts (PAN-AUTH-014), or nothing locks at all.

A locked account is released with `request authentication unlock-admin`; `show authentication locked-users` lists them.

controls.name: Management Session Idle Timeout
controls.description:
Ends an idle GUI or CLI session, closing the window in which an unattended console can be used by whoever walks past it. The device accepts 1 to 1440 minutes, or 0.

BOUNDED AT BOTH ENDS. 0 means sessions NEVER time out and is a sentinel - worse than any large number, though a naive comparison ranks it as the best possible value.

The implicit value is 60, MEASURED rather than assumed: the unconfigured form labels the field '60 (default)' - 2026-09-04, PA-5220. That matters because it decides what an untouched device reports. At 60 it is a live session an hour after the administrator walked away, which is a finding; had the implicit value been 0 it would have been the sentinel instead, and a more serious one.
controls.rationale: Administrative access to the firewall is access to every policy behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Authentication Settings > Idle Timeout.
controls.remediation: Set Idle Timeout to 10 minutes or fewer. Do not set 0, which disables the timeout entirely. The same screen's Max Session Time is a separate limit and does not substitute for this one.

queries.name: Severity: 11 to 60
queries.short_description: minutes of idle time before logout 11 to 60 — reported medium.

controls.name: API Key Lifetime Configured
controls.description:
How long a generated API key stays valid. The device accepts 1 to 525600 minutes, or 0.

The floor is ANY non-zero lifetime, so this fires on one value: 0, meaning keys never expire. A stolen key is then permanent, and the only remedy is expiring every key at once. 0 is also the implicit value - measured 2026-09-04, where the form reads '0 (default)' - so every device that has not been configured fires this.

The corpus grades longer lifetimes too (over a day medium, over a week high), but those bands sit above the floor and are unreachable while the assertion is 'configured at all'. They are kept rather than trimmed, because the scale is the corpus author's and a later tightening of the floor would want them.
controls.rationale: Administrative access to the firewall is access to every policy behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > Authentication Settings > API Key Lifetime.
controls.remediation: Set API Key Lifetime to a non-zero value; 1440 minutes (24 hours) is the common target. Changing the lifetime or the master key INVALIDATES EXISTING KEYS - coordinate with whoever owns the automation before doing it.

controls.name: Authentication Profile Failed-Attempt Lockout
controls.description:
Locks an account authenticated through this profile after N consecutive failures, extending brute-force protection to externally authenticated administrators.

BOUNDED AT BOTH ENDS, and the low end is the trap. The device accepts 0 to 10, and a 0 does not mean strict - it means UNLIMITED LOGIN ATTEMPTS. It is also the implicit value in normal operational mode, so a comparison written as 'more than 5 is a finding' passes every unconfigured profile in an estate.

A lockout-time of 0 does NOT disable this. The Web Interface Help says on p.840 that a non-zero Failed Attempts with Lockout Time 0 means the user is never locked out; that was MEASURED FALSE on 2026-09-04, three failed logins against a profile with failed-attempts 2 and lockout-time 0 locked the account until an administrator released it. The same wrong claim appears on p.707 about the device-admin lockout and was measured false there too. So this control asserts on failed-attempts alone.

Does not apply to SAML profiles: the Help prefixes both lockout fields '(All authentication types except SAML)'.

The query EXCLUDES SAML profiles rather than merely noting the exception, because a finding the platform cannot act on is a false positive. The lab has one - asdfasdf on pan-fw-111 - and it fired before the exclusion was added.
controls.rationale: Administrative access to the firewall is access to every policy behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Authentication Profile > <profile> > Advanced > Failed Attempts.
controls.remediation: Set Failed Attempts to 5 or fewer on the profile; 3 is the common hardening target. Do not leave it at 0, which permits unlimited guessing. Set a Lockout Time as well - 0 holds the account until an administrator releases it, which is stronger but is an availability decision.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Lockout disabled, or a limit looser than 3 attempts.

queries.name: Severity: 4 to 5
queries.short_description: failed attempts before lockout 4 to 5 — reported low.

queries.name: Severity: 6 to 10
queries.short_description: failed attempts before lockout 6 to 10 — reported medium.

controls.name: Multi-Factor Authentication for Administrative Access
controls.description:
DEFERRED 2026-09-10 - not derivable from configuration. Jason: "PAN-AUTH-020 is not derived from the config, lock that decision in."

PAN-OS gives an administrator a second factor only through the FIRST factor - a RADIUS server, a SAML identity provider, or the Cloud Authentication Service - and none of the three records in the firewall's configuration whether MFA is enforced on the other side. The one factor the configuration DOES show, the Factors tab, is not enforced for administrators: measured 2026-09-10, oep-mfa-admin logged in with its password alone through a profile carrying an MFA factor (PAN-AAA-011 reports that trap). The Cloud Authentication `force-mfa` key records an operator's claim about the IdP, not a check.

So a pass here would credit MFA the configuration cannot see, and a failure would fire on administrators whose MFA lives on the server. Kept in the catalog, inactive, so the model, compiler and tests remain; the evidence belongs to the RADIUS/SAML/CIE side.

Requires a second factor on the path an ADMINISTRATOR authenticates by, so a stolen password alone cannot reach the management plane.

THE FINDING IS ABOUT A PERSON, NOT A PROFILE. This was first built over AuthenticationProfile and left inactive, because a profile row cannot say which administrators are exposed: two accounts on one appliance can sit behind different profiles, and the estate's profiles also serve GlobalProtect and Captive Portal, which are separate controls. Jason, 2026-09-08, ABOUT THIS CONTROL AND PAN-AUTH-019 SPECIFICALLY: "We generate findings per user, not per profile... A row is a specific user, and its values are the value checks." So it reports one finding per administrator, on the same row as that account's other findings.

THAT IS NOT A GENERAL RULE, and he said so on 2026-09-09: the other authentication profile controls stay profile-centric. PAN-AUTH-018 asserts something about a profile's own lockout configuration and its subject is the profile. What moves a control onto the account is that its assertion is about a PERSON'S exposure, which a profile row cannot express because two administrators on one appliance can sit behind different profiles.

IT RESOLVES THROUGH TWO BINDINGS. The per-account `mgt-config/users/entry/authentication-profile` wins; otherwise the device-wide `deviceconfig/system/authentication-profile` covers the account. `admin_mfa_enabled` is the resolved profile's flag.

NO PROFILE AT ALL FIRES. An administrator on the local database has no second factor, so a stolen password alone reaches the management plane - which is exactly what this asserts. It is a separate failure from PAN-AUTH-019 (the credential is local and unrevocable) and both report on the row, because one bad thing is not excused by another.

The device enforces a prerequisite that needs no encoding: `mfa-enable` is REJECTED unless the profile already references an MFA factor, so an enabled profile always has one. A SAML profile may carry MFA at the identity provider instead, which this cannot see - that is a downgrade the assessor makes.
controls.rationale: Administrative access to the firewall is access to every policy behind it.
controls.audit: Device > Administrators > <account> > Authentication Profile, then Device > Authentication Profile > <that profile> > Factors > Enable Additional Authentication Factors. Where the account names no profile, check Device > Setup > Management > Authentication Settings.
controls.remediation: Create an MFA server profile, add it as a factor on the authentication profile, then enable Multi Factor Authentication - in that order, because the device refuses the flag without a factor. SAML profiles may carry MFA at the identity provider instead, which this control cannot see.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: No second factor governs this administrator.

controls.name: External Authentication for Administrator Accounts
controls.description:
An administrator account is centrally authenticated only when BOTH halves hold: authentication reaches an external identity service, and no credential is stored on the device. This reports every account where either fails.

A BOUND PROFILE IS NOT EVIDENCE OF CENTRALIZATION. The method matters. On the lab, three of the four accounts that passed an earlier version of this control were reaching the firewall's OWN local user database through a profile - `oep-auth-lockout` and `oep-auth-hardened` are method `local-database`, and `aegis_auth_prof` names no method at all. A control titled for external authentication was passing accounts that do not use it. External means RADIUS, TACACS+, LDAP, Kerberos, SAML or Cloud.

A STORED CREDENTIAL STILL COUNTS EVEN WHERE A PROFILE IS BOUND. Measured 2026-09-08 as an A/B on one account: with its authentication profile unbound it authenticated; with the same password and the profile bound back a minute later it was refused, and the device logged the profile and its unreachable server. A per-account profile takes precedence and the local password is not tried. So the credential is unreachable while the binding holds - and it is still a secret that leaves with a configuration backup, and becomes live the moment somebody removes the profile. Latent, the way a password profile that weakens the global policy is a latent exemption. Jason, 2026-09-08: "mfa/external=yes and local phash=no".

BOTH CREDENTIAL KINDS COUNT. The corpus note names `phash` only; an SSH public key in the same config is exactly as local. pan-fw-111's `azureuser` carries no password at all and is a superuser reachable by a key nobody centrally holds.

The DEVICE-WIDE binding `deviceconfig/system/authentication-profile` is honoured when the account names no profile of its own, and it is a different mechanism from the per-account one. Measured 2026-09-08 with both device-wide leaves pushed at an unreachable server, two attempts two seconds apart: an account with NO credential was sent to the profile and timed out, while an account holding a stored password authenticated locally and the profile was never consulted for it. So it covers exactly the accounts that have no local credential - which is why resolving through it is right, and why an account holding a password is not excused by it.

`client-certificate-only` clears nothing. Web Interface Help p.825 scopes it to the web interface - "Use only client certificate authentication (web)" - and it neither replaces the stored credential nor centralizes the account.

This is a POSTURE control. A break-glass account is a legitimate reason for one of these to exist, and an assessor gives it; the control's job is to put every one of them in front of somebody, not to decide which are documented. That reading is reinforced by the other edge of the precedence measurement: when the AAA server is down, nobody bound to it per-account can log in at all.
controls.rationale: A credential that exists only on the device is one no joiner-mover-leaver process can reach.
controls.audit: Device > Administrators > <account> > Authentication Profile, then Device > Authentication Profile > <that profile> > Authentication > Type. Check the account's Password and SSH key while you are there.
controls.remediation: Bind the account to an authentication profile whose type is TACACS+, RADIUS, LDAP, Kerberos or SAML - not `local database` and not `none` - and then remove its local password and any public key. Removing the credential is the half that gets skipped, and it is the half that survives somebody unbinding the profile later. Where an account must stay local as break-glass, vault the credential offline, alert on its use, and record the decision.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Not reached by an external identity service, or holding a device-stored credential.

controls.name: Default 'admin' Account Disabled or Replaced
controls.description:
`admin` is the username every PAN-OS device ships with and every password spray starts from. Named per-person accounts should carry day-to-day work, and the default account should be deleted or held as vaulted break-glass.

IT FIRES ON PRESENCE, AT THE CORPUS SEVERITY. Whether the password is still the factory one is not in the configuration - `phash` is a hash - so this cannot confirm the whole failure the severity describes. That is not a reason to soften it. The consultant can see the account, ask how it is held, and reduce the severity when it meets the control language; nothing downstream can raise a severity that arrived understated, so an understated one is the finding nobody looks at again.

Jason, 2026-09-08: "if an account with name 'admin' exists, it should be a critical finding. The consultant can then do the work to reduce the severity if it meets minimum control language. We can't account for that."

The corpus's `minimum_value_descr` and `preferred_value_descr` split this into a password check and a presence check, and the split does not survive contact with what a config read can see. Read the two together: the assertion is that the default account should not be sitting there.
controls.rationale: A universally known username is a free half of every credential-stuffing attempt.
controls.audit: Device > Administrators - is there an entry named `admin`, and do named superusers exist beside it?
controls.remediation: Create and TEST a named superuser first, then delete `admin`. Where it is kept as break-glass, vault the credential, bind login alerting to it, record the decision - and downgrade the finding, which is the assessor's call rather than the tool's.

controls.name: Limit Number of Superuser Accounts
controls.description:
Every superuser is a full-compromise path: the role can rewrite policy, read secrets, create further administrators and disable the logging that would show it. Day-to-day work belongs on least-privilege roles.

THE FINDING NAMES THE ACCOUNTS, NOT THE APPLIANCE. The assertion is about a count, but the remediation is per-account - somebody decides which of the seven get demoted - so each superuser reports, and they share one graded severity because they share one cause.

`superuser_cohort_size` is the appliance's superuser total written onto each superuser row, and 0 on every account holding another role. That is literally correct - a devicereader belongs to no superuser cohort - and it keeps every query on this control to ONE field, so a threshold is the only number in play. The graded severities are the two non-baseline queries below: 3 to 5 reports low, 6 to 10 reports medium, and anything above reports the control default.

Thresholds are the corpus's proposed baselines - 5 minimum, 2 preferred - and are pending sign-off.
controls.rationale: Superuser count is the size of the blast radius, and it only ever grows on its own.
controls.audit: Device > Administrators - count entries whose Administrator Type is Dynamic / Superuser.
controls.remediation: Move operators, auditors and automation onto custom admin roles scoped to what they do, and leave superuser to a named few plus break-glass. Demoting an account does not disturb how it authenticates.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: More than two superusers on this appliance.

controls.name: Unused Authentication Profiles (Hygiene)
controls.description:
An authentication profile that nothing references is configuration debt. It authenticates nobody while it stays unreferenced, but it is a definition nobody is maintaining, and binding it later applies whatever it was left holding - often a stale AAA server, or no lockout at all.

AN UNUSED CLAIM IS ONLY AS GOOD AS THE LIST OF HIDING PLACES. The CLI grammar names eight referrer paths on a firewall: the two `deviceconfig/system` leaves, per-administrator `mgt-config/users`, captive portal, GlobalProtect portal and gateway, secure web gateway, and authentication objects. Rather than visit those eight, the normalizer walks the WHOLE merged payload for the two referrer keys - a path the grammar missed would otherwise make this control report an in-use profile as unused, which is the worst direction for a hygiene control to fail in. The grammar list is kept as a cross-check on the walk.

Four of the eight have been seen carrying a real reference and confirmed readable from merged config, and they cover all four structural shapes: an appliance-level container of entries, a device leaf, a vsys leaf, and a leaf nested inside a vsys entry. The four unseen paths reuse those shapes.

A REFERENCE RESOLVES BY SCOPE. A referrer inside a vsys resolves to that vsys's profile of the name when one exists and to the shared one otherwise, so the count lands on the definition actually in use rather than on a same-named neighbour.

Reported per appliance. A profile pushed from a template exists separately in each firewall's configuration, and referenced on one device but not another is two facts about two devices.
controls.rationale: An orphaned profile is a live definition nobody audits, one binding away from being in use.
controls.audit: Device > Authentication Profile - for each profile, search the configuration for its name.
controls.remediation: Delete the profile. PAN-OS refuses a delete that would break a reference and names the referring path in the error, so a refusal is itself the answer to 'is this really unused'. Where a profile is staged for work not yet done, record that rather than leaving it to be rediscovered.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: Profiles nothing on the appliance references.

controls.name: Password Profiles Do Not Weaken Global Policy (Hygiene)
controls.description:
A password profile OVERRIDES the global Minimum Password Complexity settings for the accounts it is applied to - Web Interface Help p.822 - so it is an exemption rather than another place the same values live. This asks whether the exemption is weaker than what it replaces.

THE COMPARISON IS NOT 'profile larger than global'. Zero is a sentinel on BOTH sides: 0 means the password never expires, which is the weakest setting available rather than the strictest. The corpus note says to flag any larger value, and the lab holds exactly the case that breaks: a profile with expiration-period 365 on a device whose global is 0. Numerically larger, semantically STRONGER, and flagging it would report a profile that improves the policy.

So a profile weakens the global policy when it never expires and the global does, or when both expire and the profile's period is longer. A global of 0 cannot be weakened by anything.

The comparison is stored on the row rather than expressed as a query, because the search layer compares a field to a LITERAL and this is the only control in the corpus needing field-to-field. Both operands are kept as columns so the conclusion can be checked rather than taken.

The corpus also asks to flag the ACCOUNTS assigned such a profile. That needs the administrator model and is enrichment for the remediation, not part of the assertion - a profile that weakens policy is a latent exemption whether or not anyone holds it today. Note the platform will not let one be assigned to an account using local database authentication.
controls.rationale: An exemption nobody audited is how a hardened policy stops applying to the accounts that matter.
controls.audit: Device > Password Profiles > <profile> > Required Password Change Period, against Device > Setup > Management > Minimum Password Complexity.
controls.remediation: Either raise the global expiration period to match, or shorten the profile's Required Password Change Period so it is no longer than the global one. Setting the profile to 0 does not fix it - 0 means the password never expires, which is the weakest value available.

controls.name: Certificate Key Strength Minimums
controls.description:
Every certificate on the device must meet RSA 2048 or ECDSA P-256 as a floor. Remediation is REISSUANCE, not a configuration write - a weak key cannot be strengthened in place.

Neither the key size nor the algorithm exists in any PAN-OS configuration field. The `algorithm` field reports RSA or EC - the key algorithm, not its size - and no operational command carries the bit length either. Both are decoded from the X.509 blob PAN-OS stores under the misleadingly named `public-key`, which holds the entire certificate.

The threshold is per ALGORITHM and cannot be a single number. 256-bit EC is strong and 256-bit RSA is broken, so `key_size_bits < 2048` would flag the vendor's own TLSv1.3_Default - which is EC secp256r1 - while passing a hypothetical RSA 512. The query pairs each algorithm with its own floor.

A certificate that could not be decoded is reported, not passed. An unreadable certificate is not a compliant one.
controls.rationale: A weak key undermines every certificate that chains to it, and unlike most findings this one cannot be fixed by editing configuration - the certificate has to be reissued and redistributed, which makes early detection worth more than usual.
controls.audit: Device > Certificate Management > Certificates shows each certificate; the key size is visible in the certificate detail. Confirm RSA is 2048 or above and EC is P-256 or above.
controls.remediation: Reissue the certificate with a compliant key and replace it wherever it is referenced. For CAs and long-lived certificates the corpus prefers RSA 3072 or ECDSA P-384.

controls.name: No Weak Signature Algorithms (SHA-1/MD5)
controls.description:
A certificate signed with MD5 or SHA-1 inherits the weakness of that hash: both have practical collision attacks, and a collision is a forged certificate.

Like the key size, the signature algorithm exists in NO PAN-OS field - `algorithm` reports the key algorithm - and is decoded from the certificate itself.

MD5 is the floor and SHA-1 is reported alongside it, because the control is named for both. The corpus allows SHA-1 "only for internal legacy with a documented expiry", which is an organisational exception this cannot see: a SHA-1 finding may legitimately be closed as accepted, an MD5 finding should not be. The preferred state is SHA-256 or stronger exclusively.
controls.rationale: A signature is the only thing binding a certificate's identity to its key. A hash with practical collisions makes that binding forgeable, so the certificate proves nothing about who holds the key.
controls.audit: Read the signature algorithm on each certificate. Anything naming md5 or sha1 reports; sha256WithRSAEncryption and ecdsa-with-SHA256 or stronger pass.
controls.remediation: Reissue with a SHA-256 or stronger signature. Where a SHA-1 certificate is a documented legacy exception, record the expiry it was accepted until and close the finding against that, rather than leaving it open indefinitely.

controls.name: Certificate Profiles Enforce Revocation Checking
controls.description: Certificate profiles govern how the firewall validates peer certificates - admin certificate authentication, GlobalProtect client certificates, SAML, syslog TLS. CRL or OCSP checking must be enabled, or a revoked credential keeps working until it expires.\n\nEither leaf satisfies the floor. Measured 2026-09-02 from the blank Add Certificate Profile form: use-crl and use-ocsp both default to DISABLED, as do all four block-* options, so a profile that sets nothing performs no revocation checking at all. That uniformity is worth knowing rather than assuming - on the management plane, server-verification absent means ENABLED while its neighbour means disabled.
controls.rationale: Revocation is the only mechanism that withdraws trust from a credential before it expires. Without it, a compromised administrator certificate remains valid for its full lifetime no matter how quickly the compromise is detected.
controls.audit: At Device > Certificate Management > Certificate Profile, confirm each profile has Use CRL or Use OCSP ticked. Note that OCSP takes precedence over CRL where both are on, as the dialog states.
controls.remediation: Enable Use OCSP with Use CRL as fallback, and set Block session if certificate status is unknown and Block session if certificate status cannot be retrieved within timeout - without those, a failed check is indistinguishable from a passed one.

controls.name: SSL/TLS Service Profiles Enforce TLS 1.2 Minimum
controls.description:
SSL/TLS service profiles set the protocol floor for every service terminating TLS on the device: management UI, GlobalProtect portal and gateway, Captive Portal, syslog. TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are formally deprecated by RFC 8996.

This control asserts the FLOOR and nothing else, which is what the corpus specifies. It is worth being explicit about what that leaves out: measured 2026-09-02, an absent algorithm key means ENABLED, so a profile carrying only a version range permits SHA-1 authentication and CBC encryption. Every profile in the lab does. Those settings are collected and shown beside the floor so an engineer can see them, and no control fires on them yet.

Assessed per profile per appliance per SCOPE. A name is not unique on a device - TLSv1.3_Default exists as both a predefined and a shared entry - and the predefined definition is the one in force.
controls.rationale: A profile is reusable by design, so a weak floor set once is inherited by every service that binds it. Auditing the bound profile alone misses the profile that is about to be bound.
controls.audit: At Device > Certificate Management > SSL/TLS Service Profile, confirm Min Version is TLSv1.2 or higher on every profile, not only the one bound to the management interface.
controls.remediation: Set Min Version to TLSv1.2 on each profile, or TLSv1.3 where every client supports it. Consider also unticking SHA1 and the CBC encryption algorithms, which are enabled by default and are not covered by this control.

controls.name: Management Certificate Issued by Trusted CA
controls.description:
The management UI certificate should chain to an organisation-trusted CA rather than the factory self-signed certificate, so administrators can detect man-in-the-middle interception of management sessions.

Split from PAN-MGT-010 because the protocol floor and the certificate are independent and have different remediations. Measured 2026-09-02: the shipped TLSv1.3_Default profile - the obvious fix for PAN-MGT-010 - carries /config/predefined/certificate's TLSv1.3_Default, which is the device's OWN factory certificate, common-name equal to the chassis serial and self-signed. Remediating PAN-MGT-010 the easy way therefore leaves this control failing, which is exactly why it is its own control.

What is decidable here is CA-ISSUED versus SELF-SIGNED, from PAN-OS's own subject and issuer hashes. Whether the issuing CA is the ORGANISATION'S is not a configuration fact and this control does not claim to decide it - the issuer is reported so a human can. A CA-issued certificate from an unexpected authority will pass and still deserve attention, and the corpus's preferred state goes further still: an internal-CA certificate whose SAN matches the management FQDN and which admin browsers already trust.

WHAT THIS CAN AND CANNOT DECIDE. Trust is not readable from configuration - there is no trust store here - so this classifies the ISSUER CHAIN as far as the device shows it. A chain terminating at a self-signed CA that is itself on the device is a PRIVATE root: nothing trusts it by default, and a browser rejects it exactly as it rejects a self-signed leaf. A chain that leaves the device may reach a public root, which cannot be confirmed here and is not claimed.

That distinction was previously collapsed, and the collapse hid a real case: a certificate signed by a lab CA created minutes earlier classified as CA-issued and PASSED, while Chrome refused the same chain with NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID. The control was named for trust and asserted only 'not self-signed'.

The private-CA case is graded DOWN from the self-signed one rather than treated as equal. An organisation's own internal CA is also private, and a certificate it issued is a different conversation from one the device signed for itself - the remediation is to distribute the root or move to a public CA, not to stop using self-signed certificates. Jason, 2026-09-07.

THIS SEVERITY SCALE IS LOCAL, not from the corpus. controls.json carries no scale for this control; the bands below were added with the classification they grade.
controls.rationale: A self-signed management certificate trains administrators to click through browser warnings, which is precisely the reflex a man-in-the-middle on the management network depends on. The warning is the only thing distinguishing the real device from an impostor, and it stops being a signal once it is always present.
controls.audit: Confirm the SSL/TLS service profile bound at Device > Setup > Management > General Settings names a certificate whose Issuer differs from its Subject, and that the issuer is an authority the organisation recognises. Device > Certificate Management > Certificates shows both.
controls.remediation: Issue a certificate for the management interface from the organisation's CA, import it under Device > Certificate Management > Certificates, and reference it from the bound SSL/TLS service profile. Where no profile is bound yet, PAN-MGT-010 must be remediated first - the certificate is carried by the profile.

queries.name: Severity: private_ca
queries.short_description: issuer chain of the management certificate private_ca — reported low.

controls.name: Master Key Changed from Default
controls.description:
The master key encrypts every private key and stored secret on the device. The factory default is a PUBLICLY KNOWN value, so a firewall that never set one is protecting its key material with a shared secret anybody can look up - including the private keys behind its certificates.

Detected from `show system masterkey-properties`. An `expire-at` of 0 - which the CLI renders as 'unspecified' - means no key was ever set. The inference is that a lifetime is MANDATORY when setting one, in both the CLI and the GUI, so a key that has been set always carries a concrete expiry.

The corpus names this control '...and Rotated'. One test covers both halves: a concrete expiry means a key was set AND that a lifetime exists for it, so there is a rotation schedule. What cannot be established is WHEN it was changed - expire-at minus lifetime breaks when auto-renew is non-zero, since the expiry moves without the key changing - nor by whom, since no attribution field exists anywhere.
controls.rationale: Every other cryptographic control on the device rests on this one. A hardened SSL/TLS profile with a CA-issued certificate protects nothing if the private key behind it is encrypted with a value published in vendor documentation.
controls.audit: Run `show system masterkey-properties`. Expiry and reminder reading 'unspecified' means the default key is still in use. Concrete dates mean a key has been set.
controls.remediation: Set a master key at Device > Master Key and Diagnostics, or with `request master-key new-master-key <value> lifetime <hours>`, and store the value in the organisation's secret manager - it is unrecoverable and required to restore a configuration. Note this re-encrypts all key material through an auto-commit, and on an HA pair both members must carry the same key. From PAN-OS 12.2.2 this stops being optional: the device starts a 60-day grace period on detecting the default key, after which commits FAIL and HA sync is suspended.

controls.name: Weak Algorithms Excluded from SSL/TLS Service Profiles
controls.description:
An SSL/TLS service profile controls far more than its protocol floor. It also selects the key exchange, encryption and authentication algorithms every service that binds it will negotiate, and ABSENT MEANS ENABLED - measured 2026-09-02 from a profile writing only a version range, whose every algorithm box renders ticked.

So a profile can satisfy PAN-CRT-005 with a TLS 1.2 floor and still permit SHA-1 authentication, CBC-mode encryption and static RSA key exchange. Every profile in the lab does.

This control asserts the MINIMUM, matching how the corpus draws that line on every other cryptographic surface: PAN-IKE-004 and PAN-IPS-003 exclude MD5 and SHA-1, PAN-MCR-003 requires SHA-2, PAN-DCP-002 removes 3DES, RC4 and MD5. SHA-1 is the only primitive of that class an SSL/TLS service profile can select, so it is the floor here. The preferred state goes further - AEAD ciphers only and ECDHE only, which is exactly PAN-DCP-002's preferred wording - and is remediation guidance rather than a second assertion.

Profiles capped at TLS 1.3 are EXCLUDED. TLS 1.3 removed CBC, static RSA and SHA-1 from its cipher suites, so these settings cannot apply to a 1.3-only handshake. That is inferred from the protocol specification and NOT measured on the device - the checkboxes remain visible on such a profile - but firing on the vendor's own TLSv1.3_Default would be a false positive on the strongest profile PAN-OS ships.
controls.rationale: A profile is reusable by design, so weak algorithms selected once are inherited by every service that binds it - management UI, GlobalProtect, Captive Portal, syslog. And because absent means enabled, this is the state a profile arrives in by default: an administrator who sets only a version floor has not narrowed the algorithms at all, and the configuration gives no sign of it.
controls.audit: At Device > Certificate Management > SSL/TLS Service Profile, open each profile and read the Authentication Algorithms group. SHA1 must be unticked. Note that an unconfigured profile shows every box ticked, so nothing having been changed is the failing state rather than a neutral one.
controls.remediation: Untick SHA1 under Authentication Algorithms. For the preferred state also untick the CBC encryption algorithms, leaving AES-GCM and CHACHA20-POLY1305, and untick RSA under Key Exchange Algorithms so that only DHE and ECDHE remain, which gives forward secrecy. Verify client compatibility first: removing CBC and static RSA breaks very old clients, which is why they are the preferred state rather than the floor.

controls.name: SSH Management Ciphers Restricted to Strong Algorithms
controls.description:
Restricts the management SSH server to AES-128-CTR or stronger. The only weaker ciphers PAN-OS can offer are the three CBC modes, selectable in a profile; the default offer contains none, so this fires only on a profile that adds one.

The subject is what the management SSH server OFFERS: the bound profile's list where it sets one, and the device's built-in default where it does not - measured 2026-09-11 on 11.1 (PA-5220) and 11.2 (PA-VM), identical. A profile that sets only some lists leaves the others at the default. A bound profile is not in force until the SSH service restarts (`set ssh service-restart mgmt`), which the configuration does not record, so a finding describes the configured offer.
controls.rationale: CBC-mode SSH ciphers are exposed to plaintext-recovery attacks that CTR and GCM are not.
controls.audit: Device > Certificate Management > SSH Service Profile - the profile bound under Device > Setup > Management > SSH Management Profiles: Ciphers.
controls.remediation: Remove aes128-cbc, aes192-cbc and aes256-cbc from the bound profile, commit, then run `set ssh service-restart mgmt`.

controls.name: SSH Key Exchange Algorithms Restricted
controls.description:
The management SSH server's key exchange must be restricted to an explicit list. With no SSH management profile bound - or a bound profile whose KEX list is absent OR EMPTY - the device advertises its entire built-in set: curve25519, the NIST ECDH curves, group-exchange-sha256, group16-sha512, group14-sha256 and diffie-hellman-group14-sha1. Measured 2026-09-11 on 11.1 (PA-5220) and 11.2 (PA-VM), identical; an explicitly empty `<kex/>` commits and offers exactly what an absent list does. Jason, 2026-09-11: "we fire if KEX is missing."

Nothing weaker than group14-sha1 is selectable in a profile or in the measured default, so the failure is the ABSENCE of a restriction rather than a weak value inside one. A configured list that still includes group14-sha1 - SHA-1 key exchange, which RFC 9142 calls deprecated and a last resort - reports at low, a preferred-state gap against the ECDH curves PAN-OS marks recommended.

A bound profile is not in force until the SSH service restarts (`set ssh service-restart mgmt`), which the configuration does not record, so a finding describes the configured offer.
controls.rationale: An unrestricted SSH server negotiates whatever the client asks for, SHA-1 key exchange included.
controls.audit: Device > Setup > Management > SSH Management Profiles - the bound server profile's KEX list (Device > Certificate Management > SSH Service Profile). No profile, or no KEX list in it, means every KEX the device supports.
controls.remediation: Bind an SSH management profile whose KEX list is ecdh-sha2-nistp256/384/521, commit, then run `set ssh service-restart mgmt`.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: No KEX restriction - the device advertises its whole default set.

queries.name: Severity: configured list includes group14-sha1
queries.short_description: Restricted, but diffie-hellman-group14-sha1 is still in the list.

controls.name: SSH MAC Algorithms Restricted
controls.description:
Restricts session integrity to HMAC-SHA2. The device default offers hmac-sha1, hmac-sha1-etm and umac-64/128 alongside SHA-2, so an appliance with no profile - or one whose profile leaves MACs unset - fires, as does a profile that selects hmac-sha1.

The subject is what the management SSH server OFFERS: the bound profile's list where it sets one, and the device's built-in default where it does not - measured 2026-09-11 on 11.1 (PA-5220) and 11.2 (PA-VM), identical. A profile that sets only some lists leaves the others at the default. A bound profile is not in force until the SSH service restarts (`set ssh service-restart mgmt`), which the configuration does not record, so a finding describes the configured offer.

SEVERITY is the corpus band, converted to a query: any MAC below SHA-2 reports at the control's medium; a server offering only SHA-2 but still including hmac-sha2-256 reports at low, a preferred-state gap against hmac-sha2-512.
controls.rationale: SHA-1 and 64-bit UMAC tags are below the SHA-2 floor for session integrity.
controls.audit: The bound SSH management profile's MAC list, or the device default when none is bound or the list is unset.
controls.remediation: Bind an SSH management profile whose MAC list is hmac-sha2-512 (and hmac-sha2-256 for compatibility), commit, then run `set ssh service-restart mgmt`.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: A MAC other than HMAC-SHA2 is offered.

queries.name: Severity: weakest MAC hmac-sha2-256
queries.short_description: SHA-2 only, but hmac-sha2-256 is still offered - meets the floor, misses the preferred hmac-sha2-512.

controls.name: Strong SSH Host Key
controls.description:
The management SSH server authenticates itself to administrators with ONE host key - the default type only, measured 2026-09-11: tpa-b, whose profile sets ECDSA 256, offers ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 and nothing else, while the untouched devices offer RSA (2048, read off the wire with ssh-keyscan).

RAISED ABOVE THE CORPUS MINIMUM, deliberately. controls.json says the default RSA 2048 "meets the floor for authenticating the device to administrators; no change required", which leaves the control with no reachable failure - every selectable value is at least 112-bit. This fires at the 128-bit floor instead: RSA below 3072 bits. RSA 2048 is 112-bit strength, which NIST SP 800-131A Rev.3 and IR 8547 (both drafts) deprecate for signatures after 2030, and PAN-OS's own documentation recommends the ECDSA 256 key. A consultant who disagrees can lower it; a control that can never fire cannot be argued with at all.

ECDSA at any offered size (256/384/521) passes, as does RSA 3072 or 4096. Key ROTATION is not assessed: the configuration records the key's type and size, never its age.

The subject is the management SSH server's effective configuration: the bound profile's value where it sets one, the device default where it does not - measured 2026-09-11 on 11.1 and 11.2. A bound profile is not in force until `set ssh service-restart mgmt`, which the configuration does not record.
controls.rationale: An RSA 2048 host key is 112-bit strength, deprecated for signatures after 2030; ECDSA 256 is 128-bit and is what PAN-OS recommends.
controls.audit: Device > Certificate Management > SSH Service Profile > Hostkey, on the profile bound under Device > Setup > Management. Unset means RSA 2048.
controls.remediation: Set the bound profile's host key to ECDSA 256 (or RSA 3072+), commit, then run `set ssh service-restart mgmt`. Regenerating a host key keeps the existing type, so the type has to be set here. Administrators' known_hosts entries change.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: An RSA host key below 3072 bits - 112-bit strength.

controls.name: SSH Session Rekeying Configured
controls.description:
Rekeying bounds how much traffic one session key protects. PAN-OS offers three triggers - data volume, time interval and packet count - and whichever is reached first rekeys. Only the TIME INTERVAL is assessed, and its default is no time-based rekeying at all (Help p.905): this fires when no interval is set.

RFC 4253 section 9 recommends rekeying after one gigabyte or one hour, whichever comes sooner. The interval's configurable range is 10 to 3600 seconds, so every settable value meets the hour; 'configured' is the whole assertion and no threshold comparison is needed. The data trigger is not assessed: its default is the cipher's own limit of 1-4 GB, and an interactive management session rarely moves a gigabyte, so the interval is the trigger that acts.

NOT A FIPS-CC CHECK. The guide's rekeying REQUIREMENT (p.1308, p.1310) is about the HA1 control link in FIPS-CC mode, not the management SSH server, and HA profiles are not modelled here. A firewall in FIPS-CC mode with an unconfigured HA1 rekey is a different finding this control does not make.

The subject is the management SSH server's effective configuration: the bound profile's value where it sets one, the device default where it does not - measured 2026-09-11 on 11.1 and 11.2. A bound profile is not in force until `set ssh service-restart mgmt`, which the configuration does not record.
controls.rationale: With no time-based rekey, one session key protects a management session for its whole life.
controls.audit: Device > Certificate Management > SSH Service Profile > Interval, on the bound profile. Unset means no time-based rekeying.
controls.remediation: Set the bound profile's rekey Interval (10-3600 seconds; 3600 matches RFC 4253), commit, then run `set ssh service-restart mgmt`.

queries.name: Baseline
queries.short_description: No time-based rekey interval is set.

controls.name: Disable Telnet on Management Surfaces
controls.description: Telnet transmits credentials and session content in cleartext. It must remain disabled; SSH is the only acceptable CLI transport. Every management surface - MGT, Aux-1, Aux-2, and any layer-3 interface carrying an interface-management-profile - is assessed, because the risk is the same wherever the service is exposed.
controls.rationale: Telnet exposes administrator credentials and session content to anyone able to observe the path, and a management surface is by definition reachable by administrators.
controls.audit: Review each management surface and verify Telnet is not enabled. Telnet is disabled by default on current releases, so a finding means it was deliberately re-enabled.
controls.remediation: Disable Telnet on the surface reporting it and use SSH instead.

controls.name: Disable HTTP on Management Surfaces
controls.description: Unencrypted HTTP management exposes credentials and session tokens. HTTPS must be used instead. Every management surface - MGT, Aux-1, Aux-2, and any layer-3 interface carrying an interface-management-profile - is assessed, because the risk is the same wherever the service is exposed.
controls.rationale: HTTP management carries administrator credentials and session cookies in cleartext, and offers no assurance that the device being managed is the intended one.
controls.audit: Review each management surface and verify HTTP is not enabled. HTTP is disabled by default, so a finding means it was deliberately re-enabled.
controls.remediation: Disable HTTP on the surface reporting it and use HTTPS instead.

controls.name: Restrict Management Access to Permitted IP Addresses
controls.description: Limits which source addresses may reach a management surface. A surface with no permitted-source list accepts any host that can route to it. Every management surface - MGT, Aux-1, Aux-2, and any layer-3 interface carrying an interface-management-profile - is assessed, because the risk is the same wherever the service is exposed.
controls.rationale: Restricting permitted IP addresses reduces exposure of the management plane and limits administrative access attempts to trusted networks or jump hosts.
controls.audit: Review each surface's permitted-source list and verify only approved administrative networks or hosts appear. An absent or empty list means unrestricted.
controls.remediation: Configure permitted IP addresses using approved management subnets or jump-host addresses. Avoid broad ranges unless explicitly justified.

controls.name: Administrative Services on Data-Plane Interfaces
controls.description:
Every data-plane interface with an administrative service enabled is reported, so that those facing untrusted networks can be identified. Management on a data-plane interface bypasses the management-plane isolation model.

This control enumerates rather than judges. Whether an interface faces an untrusted network cannot be determined from configuration - a zone name carries no trust semantics the device enforces - so the finding states a fact and the assessor decides. Only the five administrative services raise a finding; ping, response pages, HTTP-OCSP and the User-ID listeners are reachability and service functions and are reported as context.
controls.rationale: An administrative service on a data-plane interface is reachable from whatever that interface faces, which may include untrusted or Internet-facing networks. The management-plane isolation model assumes administration arrives on the management plane.
controls.audit: Review each reported interface. Confirm the interface does not face an untrusted network, or that the exposure is operationally required and restricted by a permitted-source list.
controls.remediation: Remove the interface management profile, or reduce it to the services actually required and bind a permitted-source list.

controls.name: Login Banner Configured
controls.description: A login banner presented before authentication states who may use the device and that use is monitored. Absent, an administrator sees nothing before the prompt.\n\nThe wording is site-specific and legal rather than technical, so this control asserts only that a banner exists. Whether it carries approved language is an interview question, not a configuration one.
controls.rationale: A banner is the notice that makes unauthorised use provable in many jurisdictions, and several frameworks require one before any authentication prompt.
controls.audit: Confirm a login banner is present and carries organisation-approved wording.
controls.remediation: Set Device > Setup > Management > Login Banner.

controls.name: Force Admins to Acknowledge Login Banner
controls.description:
Requires an administrator to positively acknowledge the login banner rather than read past it.

Reported wherever acknowledgement is off, including on a device with no banner. PAN-OS greys the setting out until a banner exists, so remediating this one may mean setting a banner first - which is PAN-MGT-007, and the two are reported independently rather than one standing in for the other.
controls.rationale: Acknowledgement converts a passive notice into a recorded action by the administrator, which is what gives the banner evidentiary weight.
controls.audit: Confirm administrators must acknowledge the banner before proceeding.
controls.remediation: Enable Force Admins to Acknowledge Login Banner. The setting is unavailable until a login banner is configured, so set the banner first where there is none.

controls.name: Verify Update Server Identity
controls.description: Validates the update server's TLS certificate before content is downloaded, so a man-in-the-middle cannot deliver tampered content updates.\n\nEnabled by default: absent from configuration means ON, measured 2026-09-01. A finding here therefore means it was deliberately turned off.
controls.rationale: Content updates are executable inputs to inspection. Accepting them from an unauthenticated server undermines every signature-based control on the device.
controls.audit: Confirm Verify Update Server Identity is enabled.
controls.remediation: Enable Device > Setup > Services > Verify Update Server Identity.

controls.name: Harden Management Interface TLS Protocol
controls.description:
Binds an SSL/TLS service profile to the management web interface so administrative sessions negotiate TLS 1.2 or better.

Scope is the PROTOCOL FLOOR only. The certificate that profile presents is PAN-CRT-006, and the two are genuinely independent: the shipped TLSv1.3_Default profile satisfies this control and still serves the device's own self-signed factory certificate, so passing here says nothing about trust.

Absence is a finding, not a default pass. Measured 2026-09-02 by negotiation: with no profile bound, a PA-5220 management interface accepts TLS 1.1 and refuses only TLS 1.0. Binding a profile is what raises the floor.

The profile name resolves over two scopes, and PREDEFINED BEATS SHARED. A custom profile written under the shipped name TLSv1.3_Default is ignored entirely, settings and certificate alike, so the name alone does not tell you what is in force.
controls.rationale: The management interface carries full administrative authority, and TLS 1.1 has no acceptable modern cipher suites. An unbound interface is not merely unhardened: it is measurably weaker than the hardened profile PAN-OS already ships and could have bound for free.
controls.audit: Confirm an SSL/TLS service profile is bound at Device > Setup > Management > General Settings, and that the profile it resolves to sets Min Version to TLS 1.2 or higher. Where the bound name matches a predefined profile, read the PREDEFINED definition - a same-named custom profile is not in force.
controls.remediation: Bind an SSL/TLS service profile with Min Version TLS 1.2 at Device > Setup > Management > General Settings > SSL/TLS Service Profile. The shipped TLSv1.3_Default profile satisfies this control on its own. It does NOT satisfy PAN-CRT-006, because the certificate it carries is the device's own self-signed one.

controls.name: Enable Log on High DP Load
controls.description: Logs a system event when dataplane CPU is sustained at a high level - an early signal of flooding, decryption overload, or a device outgrowing its sizing.\n\nDisabled by default: absent from configuration means OFF, measured 2026-09-01, so an untouched device reports this finding.
controls.rationale: Sustained high dataplane load degrades inspection before it degrades throughput, and without this event the first symptom is usually a user complaint.
controls.audit: Confirm Enable Log on High DP Load is set.
controls.remediation: Enable Device > Setup > Management > Logging and Reporting Settings > Log Export and Reporting > Enable Log on High DP Load.

controls.name: Unused Interface Management Profiles
controls.description: An interface management profile that no interface references is configuration debt. It grants no access while it stays unbound, but it is a definition nobody is maintaining, and binding it later applies whatever it was left enabling.\n\nReported per appliance. A profile pushed from a Panorama template exists separately in each firewall's configuration, and bound on one device but unbound on another is two different facts about two devices.
controls.rationale: Unused definitions accumulate, are not reviewed with the configuration that is in use, and are the most likely thing to be bound by mistake or in haste. Removing them reduces what has to be read to understand how a device is administered.
controls.audit: Review each reported profile and confirm no interface references it. A profile kept deliberately for a planned change is an accepted finding rather than a defect.
controls.remediation: Delete the profile, or bind it to the interface it was created for.

controls.name: Anti-Spyware Profile Blocks Critical/High/Medium Severity
controls.description:
Anti-spyware signatures detect command-and-control, credential theft and post-exploitation beaconing. Critical and high severities must be blocked; leaving them at alert turns C2 detection into a log entry while the channel stays open.

WHAT IS ASSESSED. Every custom Anti-Spyware profile - local vsys, local shared, and Panorama-pushed - and the predefined `default` and `strict` profiles WHEN a rule or profile group uses them (Jason, 2026-09-11). An unused predefined profile protects nothing; the shipped `default` protecting a rule is the commonest weak configuration there is.

THE VERDICT IS ORDER-INDEPENDENT. A severity is blocked only when a catch-all rule covers it - any threat name, any category - and every rule that can match it takes a blocking action. No document says whether profile rules are first-match, and this reading does not need to know: it cannot pass a weak profile. Its cost is that a non-blocking rule BELOW a broad blocking one still fails the severity.

BLOCKING is drop, reset-client, reset-server, reset-both or block-ip. The corpus minimum names reset-both alone; any blocking action passes here (Jason, 2026-09-11). `default` is NOT blocking - a signature's default action is typically alert or reset-both (Web Interface Help p.272), so it cannot be relied on, and the predefined `default` profile is exactly that case.

Fires when critical OR high is not blocked, which is the corpus minimum. Medium is the corpus PREFERRED value: it is on the row and queryable, and fires nothing.
controls.rationale: Critical and high severity signatures that only alert turn detection into a log entry while the attack proceeds.
controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > Anti-Spyware > <profile> > Rules, and which Security policy rules and Security Profile Groups reference it.
controls.remediation: Give the profile a catch-all rule for critical and high severity with a reset or drop action, and remove or tighten any rule that alerts on those severities. For a predefined profile, point the rules and groups using it at `strict` or at a custom profile instead - predefined profiles cannot be edited.

controls.description:

WHAT IS ASSESSED. THE VERDICT IS ORDER-INDEPENDENT. Fires when critical OR high is not blocked, which is the corpus minimum. Medium is the corpus PREFERRED value: it is on the row and queryable, and fires nothing.

controls.audit: Objects > Security Profiles > Vulnerability Protection > <profile> > Rules, and which Security policy rules and Security Profile Groups reference it.
